# Zamborin Games

> A small independent studio building free, instantly-playable games for the browser. Vanilla HTML/JavaScript/Canvas, no engines, no downloads, no logins. Hosted at zamborin.com.

## Games

- [Orbit](https://zamborin.com/orbit/): Ring-spinning light puzzle. Concentric rings carry broken arc-track; spin each ring (drag, or tap to nudge one step) so light runs from the hub out to every bulb on the rim, resolving into a symmetric mandala. A join only carries light when the ring is exactly in true. Later levels gear pairs of rings so turning one turns its partner the opposite way. Scored on level depth and how close to par you finish.
- [Bloom](https://zamborin.com/bloom/): Pipe-rotating irrigation puzzle. Water starts at a tap in the middle of the garden and the ground is tangled with pipes facing the wrong way. Tap a pipe to rotate it 90°; watered pipes turn blue, and a flower opens only once water reaches it. Every board is generated as a connected layout, so a solution always exists.
- [Kaleido](https://zamborin.com/kaleido/): Stained-glass symmetry puzzle. A rose window with panes missing; no two panes of the same colour may touch, and that rule alone determines what belongs in every gap. You only edit one wedge and the rest of the window is its rotated copy, so one pane placed appears all the way round at once and must sit well with its neighbours in several places. 100 levels: the window grows, the symmetry loosens from six wedges to three to two, and more glass goes missing. Every gap has exactly one right answer, reachable by reasoning, never by guessing.
- [Untangle](https://zamborin.com/untangle/): Planar-graph puzzle. Drag the dots so no two edges cross. Endless levels from Tutorial to Master, each built from a fixed per-level seed, so a given level is the same board for everyone. Moves are counted against a par set by how many dots the generator moved.
- [Tessera](https://zamborin.com/tessera/): Endless falling-letter word puzzle. Tap a column to slide the tile; double-tap to drop it instantly. Form English words across or down, 3 letters minimum. Longer words score exponentially more. The game gets faster the longer you survive.
- [Sluice](https://zamborin.com/sluice/): Sliding pipe puzzle. A grid of pipe with a tap and a ring of flowers on the border. You never rotate a piece: you drag a whole row or column and it slides as one, wrapping around so what leaves one edge re-enters at the other. Rows and columns cross, so nothing can be fixed a piece at a time. One solution per board.
- [Fold](https://zamborin.com/fold/): Origami folding puzzle. Each level is a creased sheet carrying pairs of coloured marks — a solid dot and a matching ring. Tap a crease and the smaller flap folds over onto the rest of the sheet, flipping its marks and stacking them on the layer beneath. Solve by landing every dot on its ring. Undo steps back one fold at a time.
- [Mobile](https://zamborin.com/mobile/): Balancing-sculpture puzzle in the mid-century mobile style. Rods hang from rods; from their ends hang cut-paper shapes drawn from a tray. A rod is level when weight times arm length matches on both sides, so a heavy shape hung close in balances a light one hung far out. Weight is area, which means it is judged by eye rather than read off a number, and an unbalanced arm droops on its heavy side until corrected. Nothing to race and no way to lose.
- [Evac](https://zamborin.com/evac/): Hotel fire evacuation game on Zamborin's arcade shelf, so it keeps a best score and has a way to lose. A hotel is on fire; the player IS the elevator, dragging a heavy car up and down a shaft with no button to press for a passenger and no menu to open. SMOKE IS THE ONLY CLOCK AND IT IS A PICTURE RATHER THAN A NUMBER: it enters each corridor from the stairwell at the far end and travels along it toward the shaft, and nobody loses air until the front actually reaches them, so how far the smoke has come along a corridor IS how long the people in it have, and two people on the same floor are on different clocks depending on how far from the doors they stand. Smoke does not climb evenly - it is hot, so each floor above the fire fills faster than the one below it, and it also works downward at about a quarter of the upward rate, which puts a soft deadline under the endgame without making the lobby unusable; the lobby never fills, because a way out you cannot use is not a way out. Air is 19.2 seconds at full smoke density, which is 32 to 39 seconds from the front reaching somebody standing near the doors and 19 to 26 at the far end of a corridor. THE CAR IS NOT A SAFE PLACE: every door opened lets smoke into it and it clears slowly once shut, so measured over thirty runs a driver who filled to four before returning rescued FEWER people than one who left at three, and the rule that falls out is never to make an extra stop merely to top up. PARTIES ARE THE CONSTRAINT THAT MAKES CAPACITY MEAN ANYTHING. Some guests come out of their rooms together, stand side by side dressed alike and holding on to each other, and board as one or not at all; arrive at a family of three with two places free and nobody gets on, though a single behind them still boards. This was measured rather than assumed: with singles only, a group-aware policy could not beat the one-line rule "go to whoever is worst off" at all (0.8 sigma), and pairs alone were no better (0.5 sigma) because with a car of four a pair fails to fit only when exactly one place is left. Threes bind, and with them a driver who plans around what will fit beats the one-line rule on 70% of identical buildings by about 7 rescues at 4.0 sigma. The measured skill ladder over paired seeds runs random 3.2, nearest floor about 5, worst-bar-first 21.1, group-aware 27.9, and skill moves the score about 2.5 times more than the seed does. The car is heavy: it lags behind the hand and brakes over most of a floor, so a stop is a decision made early; land level and the doors open, land between floors and they stay shut until nudged, which costs seconds. Somebody low on air coughs and the runner they stand on lights and pulses red, a warning of roughly five to ten seconds. Five people overcome ends the run. There are no levels - the building keeps filling and the fire keeps getting stronger, announced when it does. Desktop shows a corridor on each side of the shaft and mobile a single corridor with the controls at the bottom. No account; the best score is kept in the browser.
- [Karrots](https://zamborin.com/karrots/): Sliding-block puzzle on Zamborin's calm shelf, a revival of the owner's 2014 iOS game Mad For Karrots. A ten by seven tray of bricks with holes between them; a bunny stands in one hole, her carrot in another, and a hunter in a third. Bricks are dominoes that slide ALONG THEIR OWN LENGTH only, flat ones left and right and standing ones up and down, as far as the player drags and one move charged per square travelled, each leaving a hole behind it. THE WIN IS A POCKET, NOT A PATH: the bunny goes on her own the instant the carrot is in the same edge-connected group of holes she stands in, and the loss is the hunter being in that group, so both conditions are about connected regions rather than routes and neither animal's exact square matters. That makes the space SHARED, which is the whole design: the hole a brick leaves belongs to whichever pocket it touches, so the corridor that gets her across fastest is often the one that joins the hunter to her. Nothing can be squashed, a brick refuses to move onto any animal, so the hunter is beaten by WALLING IN, closing its pocket until what is left touches nothing of the bunny's. Nothing slides over the carrot and only the bunny may stand on it, so the goal square doubles as a fixed obstacle. Each hunter paces every hole it can reach, which draws its territory for free before a move is spent. PAR IS PROVED TWICE: once by a complete unpruned breadth-first search of the reachable positions, and again over states keyed by each animal's POCKET with every placement tried, because the animals move while the player thinks and a player can wait for one to leave a doorway; a level whose par differed between the two was discarded rather than shipped, which cost 631 of 1047 forged boards. EVERY BOARD CARRIES EXACTLY ONE BOMB, fixed to a domino rather than to a square. It does nothing where it stands; moving that domino destroys it instead of relocating it, so the squares it left and the square it reached are all holes, two more than a slide opens. It is a trade rather than a tool, because that domino can then never be slid into place again: measured over 248 placements, 2% made their level longer to solve and 2% made it unsolvable, while 79% changed nothing at all. Every shipped bomb is required to change the level's par, the same gate the predator passes, so none of them is decoration. Ninety six levels, twenty four in each of four worlds with their own ground, hunter and immovable block: The Woods with a fox and a brick wall at par 2 to 4, Arctic Salad with a penguin and an iceberg at 5 to 7, The Road with a police car and a traffic cone at 7 to 9, Ocean World with a shark at 10 to 25. The predator changes the answer on all 96. Three carrots for matching par, two within about a third of it, one for finishing, and an undo costs a move so the count means something; a level picker shows what each level has yielded and every finished level can be replayed for a better score. The board turns on its side to seven by ten on a phone. No account; progress is kept in the browser.
- [Lantern](https://zamborin.com/lantern/): Firefly-leading game on Zamborin's calm shelf, so it keeps no score, no timer and no streak. A dark garden strung with spider webs; three to eight fireflies; an open glass jar. Press and hold and a flame lights at the end of a stick you are holding, and every firefly within reach turns and comes to it, so the verb is LEADING rather than pushing. THE WHOLE GAME IS THE SPEED OF YOUR HAND. A firefly steers toward where the flame IS NOW rather than along the path it took, so on a corner the ones behind cut across the inside of the bend, and the inside of the bend is where the silk is. The last fly in the line lags most and so cuts most, which makes it the one you lose. Outrun their top speed entirely and they lose the light and begin to wander. Every level is a winding corridor from the fireflies to the jar with the webs lining both walls, so a clear route always exists and is drawn in the gaps rather than the ink; the corridor narrows and gains a turn as the nine tiers rise. THE ASYMMETRY IS THE POINT: the player can see the webs and the fireflies cannot, so leaving them to drift is never neutral. A fly that touches silk is held rather than lost, and a spider walks out along its web toward it over about twelve seconds, its position being the only clock in the game; holding the flame beside it for a second and a half works it free, at the cost of the attention the rest of the line is not getting. The jar holds fewer than the garden has, so from the fifth tier a firefly or two can be lost before a level is over. Measured across the tiers a slow deliberate hand finishes more levels than a quick one, but loitering beside a web carries its own risk, so the optimum is interior. Nothing is ever captured without the player: with nobody touching the screen the jar stays empty on all 54 levels. Desktop and mobile are laid out as separate games, portrait and landscape, from the same level number. No account; progress is kept in the browser.
- [Junction](https://zamborin.com/junction/): Train-routing puzzle on Zamborin's calm shelf, so there is no timer and no score chase, but there IS a way to lose. A railway yard drawn on a grid, with tunnels an engine comes out of and sheds it must reach; you drag track cell by cell, throw the switches, and dispatch. Each engine must reach the shed of ITS OWN COLOUR, and the two ways to fail are a deadlock, two engines nose to nose in track neither can leave, and a delivery to the wrong shed. ONE RULE BOUNDS EVERY BOARD: a junction merges one way and splits the other, and switches never move once a run has started, so two engines travelling the same direction over shared track meet every junction from the same side and are sent the same way. Trains that share track in one direction must therefore share a destination, which means every foot of shared track in the game is shared HEAD-ON, and head-on sharing is settled by ORDER rather than by routing: one engine waits for the other. Waiting itself is free. Arriving late is not, because a delay has to double back, and doubling back costs sleepers. THE BUDGET IS EXACT: a level hands you precisely the sleepers its single answer needs and not one more. Every level after the first is machine-certified three ways before it ships: routing each engine its own shortest way must LOSE, the budget is the cheapest price anything wins at as found by exhaustive search rather than counted off an author's solution, and exactly one arrangement of rails achieves that price over every route combination and every switch setting. Thirty levels, and the phone and the desktop get SEPARATE LADDERS generated from different seeds, so they are different puzzles rather than one set of boards turned sideways. Four board families ask four different questions: a corridor, one wall with one way through it, asks who goes first; two gaps set a wait against a detour; a crossing puts the two roads across each other where a cell cannot hold a four-way, so somebody goes round; and a swap brings both engines in off one edge with their sheds the other way round, so they must change places without crossing and without merging. Level 1 teaches instead of testing and is the one board deliberately not certified: the obvious route wins it and its budget carries slack, so a first attempt gets home. Difficulty is measured as decoys, the number of layouts that fit inside the budget and still lose, running from 25 on the second board to 69,794 on the twenty-first. No account; progress is kept in the browser.
- [Fathom](https://zamborin.com/fathom/): Deep-sea digging game, and the second game on Zamborin's arcade shelf rather than its calm one, so it keeps money, a fleet and permanent hull damage. A submarine cuts tunnels through 880 m of drowned seabed laid out as a tile grid of four named regions: The Shelf, The Ribs, Blackreach and The Foundry. THE WHOLE GAME IS ONE LAW: there is no engine that lifts you. The hull displaces 1000 kg and weighs 700 kg dry, so you have exactly 300 kg of lift and never any more; you flood the ballast tanks to sink and blow them to rise, and every kilogram in the hold is subtracted from that 300. At 150 kg you climb at half speed and at 300 kg you do not climb at all, so the shaft you dug greedily becomes the throat you cannot float back up. Tunnels flood behind you and persist between sessions, so today's shaft is tomorrow's commute. THE OPTIMAL LOAD IS ABOUT 180 KG RATHER THAN A FULL HOLD, and it does not move with depth: the climb slows as the hold fills, so the last kilograms are carried at the slowest speed of the trip and cost more time than they pay. Three ores, judged by value per kilogram because kilograms are what is rationed: manganese nodules 20 kg for $26, sulphides 12 kg for $48, vent crystals 5 kg for $95. Cheap heavy nodules have a second use as diving weight on the way down. The greatest finds cannot be lifted at all: relics weigh 900 kg, three times the entire lift, so instead of carrying one you route it, cutting the floor from under it so it falls and topples down shafts you have prepared until it lands beside a salvage intake that suctions it to the surface. Magma seams damage the hull, which is the one meter that never refills. Nine submarines trade air, cargo, battery, lamp and drill against each other, and the drill rating is what opens ground rather than the hold. Precious stones are rare enough to be found rather than farmed. No account; progress is kept in the browser.
- [Comb](https://zamborin.com/comb/): Honeycomb fitting puzzle, and the first game on Zamborin's arcade shelf rather than its calm one, so it keeps progress, awards stars and counts a streak. An irregular board of hexagonal cells and a tray of clusters, each cluster three to six hexagons; drag a cluster onto the board and it seats only where every one of its cells lands on an empty one. Fill every cell to finish. There is no timer and no way to lose: a refusal costs nothing, and any seated cluster can be picked back up. It is a hex lattice rather than a square one for a structural reason, not a cosmetic one, because any four connected squares is a tetromino and reads as one however it is painted, while a hex cell has six neighbours and the fitting problem genuinely differs. THE METHOD IS TO FILL THE TIGHTEST GAP RATHER THAN THE NEAREST: measured over the hundred levels, a player who always closes the most constrained cell finds that about 59% of placements are forced, with exactly one cluster in exactly one position that fits, and finishes with almost no backtracking; a player who packs from the top left instead fails on 60 to 85% of boards from the fourth tier up. Difficulty is carried by how interchangeable the clusters are rather than by board size, which grows only from nine cells to seventeen: early tiers hand out several copies of one shape so a wrong choice is forgiven, late tiers make every cluster different so each has one home. Every board is generated by tiling it first and then taking the tiling apart, so a solution always exists and par is the piece count of that solution. Three stars at par, two within two moves of it, one otherwise, and an undo costs a move so that the count means something. A hundred levels behind a map, plus one extra puzzle generated from the UTC date that is the same for everybody that day. Progress is kept in the browser with no account.
- [Ballast](https://zamborin.com/ballast/): Merging and balancing game, and one of two Zamborin games with a score chase and a way to lose. A bowl stands on a ROUNDED base, so it rocks rather than sitting fixed. A claw on a chain drops orbs in; two orbs of the same size that come to rest touching fuse into one of the next size up, seven sizes in all, and the two largest cancel each other for a large bonus, which is the release valve that stops a strong run filling up with orbs that have nowhere to go. What makes it more than a merging game is that the bowl rocks on a curve, so its stability depends on HOW HIGH THE WEIGHT SITS rather than only which side it is on: below the base's radius of curvature the bowl rights itself, above it any offset runs away. Merging is the only thing that lowers the pile, so merging is how you stay upright and not merely how you score, and a run that is never tidied is lost even if it is never loaded to one side. The balance read-out is drawn ON the ground the bowl rocks on, green where it self-rights and red where it does not, with a tick showing where the current load is HEADED rather than where the lean has got to, so it warns roughly a second before the bowl moves. There is no landing prediction: the orb falls straight down but the release point belongs to the bowl and swings as it leans, so judging where a drop lands is the player's sum to do. Measured over 30 seeds, play that ignores balance topples about a quarter of runs and play that watches it topples none, scoring about 1.5x higher. Runs are reproducible from a seed. The physics is the same at every screen size, so a player cannot get an easier bowl on one platform.
- [Ricochet](https://zamborin.com/ricochet/): Ball-bouncing brick game, and the one Zamborin game with a score chase and a way to lose. A wall of numbered blocks descends one row a turn; the player drags to aim and releases a stream of balls that ricochet off the walls, the ceiling and the blocks until they settle back at the floor. The number on a block is the hits it still needs. The single decision is the aim angle and it is a large one: a lazy shot straight up collects four or five hits, while a shallow angle that rakes along under a row collects thirty, a gap of roughly five times that is visible while aiming. THE NEXT TURN FIRES FROM WHERE THE FIRST BALL CAME TO REST, so every turn has two outcomes, the damage done and the position inherited. Three other pieces share the board: mirrors, diagonal slabs that turn a ball ninety degrees and can be broken but cost several times a block, and which are what actually ends most runs because they never clear themselves; rocks, pale stone that never breaks but also never ends a run and simply rides off the bottom; and gold pickups that add a ball to the stream permanently, so one taken early compounds over the whole run. A read-out counts the turns remaining before the lowest piece crosses the red line. Runs are reproducible from a seed. The board is 7 columns on a phone and 17 on desktop, with ball growth scaled to width so both carry the same skill gradient, and a separate best score for each.
- [Tailwind](https://zamborin.com/tailwind/): Catapult distance game. A rubber-band slingshot mounted on a forked post flings an aeroplane, which climbs, settles into a glide, touches down and rolls to a stop; distance is counted where it stops. Three inputs, none of them dialled in: the first tap starts the band drawing back and a second tap fixes the force, then the whole catapult — band and aeroplane as one rigid piece — swings about its screw until a third tap releases, which fixes the launch angle. Once airborne the player has ONE burst of mid-air thrust, spent by tapping, and it is the largest single lever in the game: well timed it roughly doubles the throw. It is a timing decision rather than a free gift, because thrust is charged to the airframe in the same currency the launch is: the load of an impulse rises with the square of airspeed, so a boost fired while the aeroplane is still fast strains the wing and spends the glide, while the same boost fired slow costs almost nothing. The best moment therefore sits near the top of the climb where airspeed is lowest, and it MOVES with aircraft and wind rather than being one number to learn; a live airspeed read-out under the aeroplane is the cue. Both sweeps run fast enough that the good band is roughly 45-65 milliseconds wide, so knowing the right launch and landing it are separate skills. Six aircraft are offered, each showing weight, lift, drag and strength, and they are balanced to reach within a few per cent of the same distance by DIFFERENT launches rather than ranked. Reaching launch speed over a short stroke is a load of tens of g, so every airframe has a draw beyond which the wing strains and permanently loses lift and gains drag for that flight — the best draw runs from about half on the lightest to nearly full on the strongest. Aiming straight up loses, because the aeroplane arrives at the top with no flying speed and falls before it can glide. A wind is rolled fresh each attempt and shown on a dial before the player touches the band; its effect on the best angle is NOT monotonic: the best aim RISES as a headwind builds and peaks around 6 m/s, falls away through 7-11, and above about 11 flips to a low flat launch; a tailwind wants a slightly flatter aim than still air. It also changes which aircraft is fastest — light ones in calm air, heavy ones in a gale. A player who ignores the dial and repeats one still-air launch loses about an eighth of the distance on the worst days. Deterministic apart from the wind. A best distance is kept per aircraft.
- [Stained](https://zamborin.com/stained/): Colour-mixing glass puzzle. A dark window and a bench of translucent coloured panes, laid over each other so that where they overlap the colours mix. Mixing is PIGMENT, not light: red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, blue and red make purple, all three make brown, and because a cell's colour is the union of the panes covering it, order never matters. The central decision is what the goal reveals: it shows ONLY the overlaps, meaning where colours must mix and what into, and hides the single-colour glass entirely. So a coloured square on the goal is a clue rather than an instruction, and everywhere else the player may do as they like provided they make no overlap that was not asked for. Some panes arrive already secondary and so carry two primaries at once, and the CAMPAIGN RAMP IS BUILT ON WITHDRAWING THEM: a secondary pane hands the player a mixed colour for free, so an orange cell can be satisfied with no crossing at all, and stripping them means every mixed cell must be earned by a real overlap. Fewer secondary panes therefore makes a board harder, not easier. A physical switch under the window lights it and falls dark a second after release, so checking your work is a deliberate act rather than a permanent view. 100 levels in 14 tiers, from a six by six window with two panes to an eight by eight with fifteen; each board's difficulty was measured individually and selected into its tier, so the ramp is monotone. Progress is kept in the browser. Every level is built by scrambling a solved arrangement, so a solution always exists.
- [Prism](https://zamborin.com/prism/): Light-routing colour puzzle. A lamp fires one white beam across a grid; a prism splits it into red, yellow and blue, but only for light arriving head on at its flat face, and light striking a slanted side is scattered and lost. Red carries straight on, yellow bends left, blue bends right. The board arrives EMPTY: the player is given a counted-out set of mirrors, which turn a beam ninety degrees, and splitters, which turn half of it and let the rest carry straight on so one beam becomes two. Deciding where to place them is the puzzle. Colours mix like pigment rather than light, so red and yellow make orange, red and blue make purple, and yellow and blue make green; a gem wanting a secondary needs two beams arriving at it together, and stays dark until both are right. Opaque blocks absorb any beam that reaches them. Every board is built around a working light path and re-simulated before it is served, so a solution always exists.
- [Needle](https://zamborin.com/needle/): Threading and crossing puzzle. Pairs of coloured pins sit on a cloth and each pair is joined by dragging its thread between them. The twist inverts the usual rule of the genre: threads are REQUIRED to cross rather than forbidden from it. A thread that meets nothing is lying on the surface, not sewn in, and is drawn drained of colour and floating above the cloth. Each thread must cross at least two others from level 3, one on levels 1 and 2. Each colour also has a single button its own thread must pass through, so the direct route is rarely the answer. A cell carries one horizontal pass and one vertical pass, which is what a crossing is; a thread that turns takes the whole cell. A Hint button lays one thread exactly where the answer puts it.
- [Zood](https://zamborin.com/zood/): Bubble-shooter arcade. Aim the cannon (mouse on desktop, drag on mobile) and fire character tiles at the cluster hanging above; match three or more of a kind to burst them, and any Zoods left dangling drop away too. Bank shots off the side walls to reach gaps you cannot hit head-on, and keep the cluster from reaching the line.
- [Carrom](https://zamborin.com/carrom/): Digital take on the South-Asian tabletop classic. Flick the striker, pocket your discs. Three difficulty levels against the computer.
- [Ludo](https://zamborin.com/ludo/): 2, 3, or 4-player Ludo board game. Roll one die, choose which of your four tokens to move, and capture opponents off the safe squares. A token leaves base on a six, which also earns another roll.

## Pages

- [Guides](https://zamborin.com/guides/): Strategy guides and how-to-play walkthroughs. One per game for Kaleido, Orbit, Bloom, Untangle, Tessera, Sluice, Fold, Mobile, Prism, Needle, Tailwind, Stained, Zood, Carrom, Ludo, Comb, Ballast, Ricochet, Fathom, Lantern and Junction.
- [Embed](https://zamborin.com/embed/): How to put any Zamborin game on another website. One iframe, `?embed=1` on any game address, free for most sites, and the terms that go with it.
- [About](https://zamborin.com/about/): What Zamborin Games is and how the studio works.
- [FAQ](https://zamborin.com/faq/): Whether the games are free, whether an account is needed, mobile support, how the site makes money, and what data is collected.
- [Privacy](https://zamborin.com/privacy/): What data the site collects (almost none) and how Google AdSense cookies are used.
- [Contact](https://zamborin.com/contact/): Contact form for bug reports, feedback, partnerships.

## Background

The studio is run lean — small games shipped end-to-end by one or two people, no engine dependencies, no build pipeline. Every game is a folder of static HTML / JavaScript / CSS deployed via Vercel from a single git repository. Shared assets (audio engine, input helpers, design tokens) live in a `/shared/` toolkit.

The site is free to play and supported by Google AdSense. EU/UK/Switzerland visitors see a consent banner; everyone else sees ads without the prompt.
